title: Ensuring multiomics data reproducibility for artificial intelligence with reference materials as a common calibrator - Nature Biotechnology
gist: A cross-institutional group led from Fudan University, with co-authors from the US FDA, IQVIA Laboratories, SAS Institute, Weill Cornell Medicine and Cellino Biotech, argues that multiomics measurements should be calibrated against reference materials co-profiled with study samples, and reported as sample-to-reference ratios, so the resulting data are reproducible enough to train and deploy artificial intelligence tools. Only the position statement is outside the paywall.

insights.claim: Reference materials should be co-profiled alongside study samples in multiomics experiments and used as a common calibrator, rather than being treated as an optional quality-control add-on.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: If adopted, this becomes a recurring consumable line item in every omics study — a demand signal for reference-material suppliers and metrology institutes.
insights.quote: Reference materials should be adopted as a common calibrator for multiomics measurement and co‑profiled with study samples.

insights.claim: Multiomics results should be reported as sample-to-reference ratios rather than as raw absolute measurements, which is a change to the reporting unit itself and not merely to normalization method.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: A ratio-based reporting standard would make historical multiomics datasets non-comparable to newly generated ones, creating switching costs and re-processing demand.
insights.quote: Multiomics results should be reported as sample‑to‑reference ratios so that they are reproducible and suitable for artificial intelligence tools.

insights.claim: The authors frame multiomics data irreproducibility as having a diagnosable root cause addressable by calibration, rather than as an irreducible property of noisy biological measurement.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Positions the problem as solvable by process and standards — which is what makes regulatory adoption plausible rather than aspirational.
insights.quote: Root cause of multiomics data irreproducibility and the role of reference materials as a common calibrator.

themes.theme: AI readiness as the forcing function

insights.claim: The argument for calibration is made specifically on the grounds of AI suitability, tying data-standards reform to the credibility of machine learning models trained on omics data rather than to classical statistics.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: AI hype is being used as leverage to push a standards change the field has resisted for years; watch for it to be adopted faster than prior QC initiatives for exactly that reason.
insights.quote: so that they are reproducible and suitable for artificial intelligence tools

themes.theme: Who is behind it and why that matters

insights.claim: The author list spans three separate US FDA units — the Office of the Commissioner, the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research and the National Center for Toxicological Research — alongside China's National Institute of Metrology, which is unusual regulatory density for a methods position piece.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
entities: Center for Drug Evaluation and Research
insights.so_what: Regulatory co-authorship is the leading indicator that a voluntary standard may become a submission expectation; omics-dependent drug and diagnostic developers should track it.

insights.claim: Corresponding authors Leming Shi and Yuanting Zheng disclose that they co-lead the MAQC Quartet and Plasmix projects, meaning the proposed calibrator standard is tied to reference-material programs they themselves run.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: The proposal has a named incumbent beneficiary — if the standard lands, the Quartet and Plasmix materials become the default reference, so track adoption of those specific programs.
insights.quote: L.S. and Y.Z. are co-leaders of the MAQC Quartet and Plasmix projects.

insights.claim: Commercial contract-research and analytics vendors are represented in the author group through IQVIA Laboratories, JMP Statistical Discovery at SAS Institute and Cellino Biotech, indicating industry buy-in beyond academia and regulators.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Service labs adopting a ratio-reporting standard would push it through the pharma supply chain faster than a journal guideline alone could.

insights.claim: The piece explicitly anchors itself to the ICH M10 guidance on bioanalytical method validation, importing a pharmaceutical regulatory framework into the discovery-omics domain.
insights.speaker: Nature Biotechnology
insights.so_what: Signals the intended end state: omics measurements held to bioanalytical-validation standards, which raises the cost and the barrier to entry for omics service providers.
